processing: Developed as a medium Wuyi oolong: partly oxidised, rolled and finished with a moderate roast that varies by maker.
harvest_season: As with other Wuyi oolongs, a spring picking; no specific timing is claimed here.
appearance_dry: Fairly uniform leaves, emerald-tinged in lighter lots and darker when roasted harder.
appearance_wet: As with other Wuyi oolongs, open leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: Creamy with a floral aftertaste in lighter makes; roasted lots are described as thick and honey-sweet.

brewing.notes: Use hot water and short steeps; go a little cooler for a light roast so the cream stays soft.

vintage_note: Usually sold by the year of the spring harvest and the level of roast, like other newer Wuyi cultivars. Lighter lots are best fresh; heavier roasts tend to benefit from a rest. Check the roast before buying, because descriptions vary a lot.
description:
Jin Fo, or Golden Buddha, is a comparatively new Wuyi oolong developed at a tea research centre on Wuyi Shan rather than selected from an old named bush.

It was shaped as a medium oolong, and the roast decides a great deal. Light lots keep a green tint in the leaf, while others are handled more like full rock teas.

That is why descriptions disagree. One account gives cream and floral aftertaste, another a thick, honey-sweet roasted body. Both may be fair to the tea they describe, so brew a small amount first, hot and short.

Ask for year and roast level, and do not confuse the name with any statement of age or status: it is a modern cultivar, not one of the old famous bushes.
history: Jin Fo was developed at the Wuyi Shan tea research centre in Fujian. Its date is less settled; one specialist retailer places the work in the 1990s, and that account has not been confirmed from the institute itself.
